summary:
What it is: A free 2D browser game where kids (under 16, designed for 10–13) act as commander of a Mars base and must survive 100 days by balancing five life-support systems.
The core idea: Kids learn about space by making tough choices. Every day they manage Air 🫁, Water 💧, Power ⚡, Food 🥬, and Shield 🛡️ (plus crew morale 😊), and events force dilemmas with no perfect answer — like your solar storm example: shut everything down and lose power overnight, or keep running and risk fried computers. After every event, a "Space Fact" card explains the real science in simple words.
Win/Lose: Survive to Day 100 → mission report. Any resource hits zero → the mission fails, and the game explains why and what a real engineer would do. Failing is a lesson, not a punishment.
Built for kids:
Grade 5 reading level, short sentences, icon-first UI
Untimed decisions, touch/tablet friendly
No accounts, no tracking, no ads (kid-privacy compliant)
details:
Our project is "Mars Outpost: Survive 100 Days" — a free 2D browser game where players command a Martian base and must keep it alive for 100 in-game days by balancing five life-support systems: Air, Water, Power, Food, and Radiation Shield. Each day brings a status report, limited Action Points for repairs and upgrades, and surprise dilemma events with no perfect answer — for example, when a solar storm hits: shut everything down (safe, but the greenhouse goes dark) or keep the power running (crops keep growing, but computers may fry). After each event, a "Space Fact" card explains the real science in plain language.

Impact: The game turns space science into decisions kids feel instead of facts they memorize. Our goal is long-term space awareness — players leave able to explain real challenges of living beyond Earth, and the game runs in any browser on cheap school computers, with a teacher guide and printable mission report for classrooms.

Tools: Built with Phaser 3, HTML/CSS/JavaScript, and Vite, with game content in data files (events.json, strings.json) so dilemmas can be added without touching code. The simulation uses pure functions, letting us auto-run thousands of simulated games to balance difficulty. The final build is a lightweight static website with local saves plus a 6-character "Mission Code."

Creativity and factors considered: Every event is a genuine trade-off, so it plays like command decisions, not a quiz. We designed for kids under 16 (Grade-5 reading level, icon-first colorblind-safe UI, no scary failure screens), for child privacy (no accounts, no ads, no tracking), and for real school conditions — old Chromebooks, tablets, and wiped saves. also see the ending it hides a surprise 😉
